A.question: What NCCN, ASCO, or ESMO clinical practice guideline recommendations or clinical trial evidence address targeted therapy for the EML4::ALK fusion in cancer? Cite the specific guideline or trial.

Guideline recommendations are written for "ALK gene fusion/ALK-positive" disease generically — EML4::ALK (the partner in ~83% of ALK-rearranged NSCLC) is not treated as a separate indication, and no society recommends a different agent based on fusion partner or EML4-ALK variant.[[1]] For advanced NSCLC, NCCN lists alectinib, brigatinib, ensartinib, and lorlatinib as preferred category 1 first-line options (ceritinib and crizotinib category 1 but "useful in certain circumstances"), and ASCO guidelines recommend alectinib, brigatinib, or lorlatinib (strong, high-quality evidence).[[2]][[3]] For resected disease, adjuvant alectinib 600 mg twice daily for 2 years is NCCN category 1 and FDA-approved based on ALINA.[[2]][[4]]
First-line therapy, advanced/metastatic NSCLC
NCCN (Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer, v2026, NSCL-27) directs patients whose ALK fusion is identified before systemic therapy to a preferred category 1 ALK TKI — alectinib, brigatinib, ensartinib, or lorlatinib (PS 0–4). Ceritinib and crizotinib remain category 1 but are listed only as useful in certain circumstances. If the fusion is discovered during first-line chemotherapy/immunotherapy, NCCN advises interrupting current therapy and starting a preferred TKI, though continuing current therapy is reasonable if the response has been good.[[2]]
ASCO guidelines (Therapy for Stage IV NSCLC with Driver Alterations, 2026) state in Recommendation 1.8 that clinicians should offer alectinib, brigatinib, or lorlatinib, and in 1.9 that ceritinib or crizotinib should be offered if those are unavailable.[[3]] The expert panel's clinical interpretation now names lorlatinib as an agent of choice when available, given durable systemic and CNS control, while noting that alectinib or brigatinib may be preferable in frail or older adults with cardiac or CNS comorbidities because of lorlatinib's higher grade ≥3 toxicity burden and need for proactive monitoring.[[3]] No head-to-head randomized comparison among these three agents exists.[[3]]
The registrational trials, all crizotinib-controlled:
[[3]][[5]][[6]][[7]][[8]]
Toxicities differ materially and should drive selection: grade 3–4 events occurred in 77% with lorlatinib vs 57% with crizotinib in CROWN, led by hypertriglyceridemia (26%), weight gain (24%), hypercholesterolemia (22%), hypertension (13%), and grade 3–4 cognitive effects (3%).[[3]] Alectinib's grade ≥3 rate was 48–58% across trials, with hyperbilirubinemia, CPK elevation, constipation, and anemia predominating.[[3]] Brigatinib requires a 7-day 90 mg lead-in before escalating to 180 mg daily because of early-onset pulmonary events, and carries a 78% grade ≥3 rate in ALTA-1L.[[3]] Ensartinib's label toxicities include rash, transaminitis, and musculoskeletal pain.[[7]]
Resected (early-stage) disease
ALINA randomized 257 patients with completely resected stage IB (≥4 cm)–IIIA (AJCC/UICC 7th ed.) ALK-positive NSCLC to alectinib 600 mg twice daily for 2 years versus four cycles of platinum doublet. DFS hazard ratio was 0.24 in both the stage II–IIIA and ITT populations; CNS DFS HR was 0.22; 4-year DFS was 75.5% vs 47.0% (HR 0.35), and OS remains immature.[[4]][[9]][[10]] Safety was manageable, with 5% discontinuation for adverse events and SF-36 quality-of-life improvement maintained over 2 years.[[11]]
NCCN lists adjuvant alectinib as category 1 for ALK-positive tumors ≥4 cm or node-positive, stages IB–IIIA and IIIB (T2–T3, N2b; T4, N2) — note this stage range extends beyond ALINA's enrolled population.[[2]] The American College of Chest Physicians 2025 early-stage guideline is more cautious, advising that alectinib be offered to high-risk patients but that chemotherapy still be discussed, since ALINA lacks long-term follow-up.[[12]] By contrast, adjuvant crizotinib was negative: ECOG-ACRIN E4512 showed no DFS benefit versus observation (HR 1.06).[[10]]
Progression on ALK TKI
NCCN separates the pathways by prior agent. After progression on alectinib, brigatinib, ceritinib, ensartinib, or lorlatinib (NSCL-28): for asymptomatic, brain-limited, or oligoprogressive disease, consider definitive local therapy (SABR, surgery, or SRS) and either continue the current TKI or switch to lorlatinib; for multifocal progression, lorlatinib if not previously given, or systemic therapy per NSCL-K.[[2]] NCCN specifies that lorlatinib is an option for resistance mutations including ALK G1202R and L1196M, but not the compound L1196M/G1202R.[[2]] After crizotinib progression (NSCL-29), any of alectinib, brigatinib, ceritinib, ensartinib, or lorlatinib may be used.[[2]] Beware TKI-discontinuation flare; restart the TKI if it occurs.[[2]]
ASCO guidelines mirror this: Recommendation 2.9 (after crizotinib) offer alectinib, brigatinib, lorlatinib, or ceritinib; Recommendation 2.10 (after alectinib or brigatinib) clinicians may offer lorlatinib, with the caveat that the supporting evidence is a single-arm phase II study in which ORR was 32.1% after one prior second-generation TKI and 38.7% after ≥2 prior ALK TKIs.[[3]] After lorlatinib failure, ASCO guidelines direct patients to platinum–pemetrexed chemotherapy, with local therapy for oligoprogression, and note ongoing trials of fourth-generation inhibitors (NVL-655, TPX-0131) active against compound mutations.[[3]]
Repeat plasma or tissue NGS at progression is recommended by both; if plasma testing is negative, tissue rebiopsy is strongly recommended, and tissue biopsy is also necessary to detect histologic (e.g., small cell) transformation, which plasma cannot identify.[[2]] NCCN acknowledges it remains unclear whether identifying a specific kinase-domain mutation reliably determines the next line of therapy.[[2]]
Immunotherapy caveat
Single-agent PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors are less effective in ALK-positive NSCLC irrespective of PD-L1 expression, and NCCN restricts first-line chemoimmunotherapy regimens and all adjuvant/perioperative checkpoint inhibitor options (atezolizumab, pembrolizumab, durvalumab, nivolumab) to patients without known ALK fusions.[[2]]
Beyond NSCLC
EML4 is the minority partner in non-lung ALK-rearranged tumors (~31%), so most of this evidence concerns other ALK fusion partners rather than EML4::ALK specifically.[[1]] Relevant guidance:
- ALK-translocated [inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor](/rare-disease/inflammatory-myofibroblastic-tumor): NCCN Soft Tissue Sarcoma (SARC-G-5) lists alectinib, brigatinib, ceritinib, crizotinib, and lorlatinib as preferred options. Crizotinib is FDA-approved for unresectable, recurrent, or refractory ALK-positive IMT in adults and children ≥1 year (adults 250 mg twice daily; pediatric 280 mg/m² twice daily), based on an [[13]]86% ORR in the COG ADVL0912 cohort. EORTC CREATE confirmed durable activity (ORR 66.7%, median PFS 18.0 months in ALK-positive patients).[[14]][[15]][[16]]
- ALK-positive systemic ALCL: crizotinib 280 mg/m² twice daily is approved for relapsed or refractory disease in pediatric patients ≥1 year and young adults — efficacy is not established in older adults. ORR was 88% with 81% CR in ADVL0912[[14]]; the French AcSé trial reported a 67% 8-week response rate with median DOR 43.3 months, but frequent relapse after discontinuation. Most ALCL cases carry NPM1::ALK rather than EML4::ALK.[[17]][[18]]
- Other tumors: ALK fusions occur in only ~0.2% of non-NSCLC cancers. NCI-MATCH subprotocol F tested crizotinib in rare ALK-rearranged tumors with an ORR of 50%, but with only five patients enrolled.[[19]][[20]]
A directly retrievable ESMO ALK-specific guideline text was not identified in this search; a 2021 secondary review characterized ESMO as grading alectinib and brigatinib as grade A and ceritinib and crizotinib as grade B first-line options, but that characterization predates the CROWN long-term data and ensartinib approval and should be verified against the current ESMO document.[[21]]

B.question: What NCCN, ASCO, or ESMO clinical practice guideline recommendations or clinical trial evidence address targeted therapy for the EML4::ALK fusion in cancer? Cite the specific guideline or trial.
B.text:
561b", "kind": "search", "label": "Searching published medical literature, guidelines, FDA, CDC, and more", "id": "searchmedicalliterature", "active": true, "children": [], "paragraphindex": 0, "metadata": {}, "queries": []}], "done": true, "summary": "Analyzed query, searched for evidence"}


EML4::ALK fusion is the defining actionable alteration in ALK-positive NSCLC, and all major guidelines recommend first-line treatment with a next-generation ALK tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI)—alectinib, brigatinib, ensartinib, or lorlatinib—based on randomized phase III trials that each demonstrated superiority over crizotinib.[[1]][[2]] EML4 and ALK both reside on the short arm of chromosome 2, and an inversion fuses them into the EML4-ALK oncogene, found in roughly 3–7% of advanced NSCLC, characteristically in younger, never/light smokers.[[3]][[4]]
NCCN Guidelines (NSCLC, v9.2026) list the following as preferred first-line options for ALK gene fusion, all category 1: alectinib, brigatinib, ensartinib, and lorlatinib.[[1]] Ceritinib and crizotinib are listed as "useful in certain circumstances" (also category 1).[[1]] If the fusion is discovered during first-line chemotherapy, the algorithm directs interruption of current therapy and initiation of a preferred ALK TKI.[[1]] The following algorithm page summarizes these first-line pathways:
[[1]]
For subsequent therapy, NCCN separates two scenarios:
- Progression on a next-generation TKI (alectinib/brigatinib/ceritinib/ensartinib/lorlatinib): options depend on symptom status and pattern of progression, and include local therapy for limited/CNS progression with continuation of the TKI, or switching to lorlatinib (if not previously given). Lorlatinib is specifically noted as an option for resistant mutations such as ALK G1202R and L1196M (except the compound L1196M/G1202R).[[1]]
- Progression on crizotinib: switch to alectinib, brigatinib, ceritinib, ensartinib, or lorlatinib, with lorlatinib reserved at later progression if not previously used.[[1]]
ASCO Living Guideline (Therapy for Stage IV NSCLC with Driver Alterations, 2026 update):[[2]]
- First line (Rec 1.8): ASCO guidelines recommend clinicians should offer alectinib, brigatinib, or lorlatinib (evidence strength high; strong recommendation). In the 2026 clinical interpretation, lorlatinib is now[[2]] positioned as an agent of choice when available given durable systemic and CNS control, while alectinib or brigatinib are reasonable alternatives—particularly in frail or older patients with cardiac/CNS comorbidities given lorlatinib's higher rate of grade ≥3 AEs.
- Rec 1.9: if those three are unavailable, offer ceritinib or crizotinib (high; strong).[[2]]
- Second line (Rec 2.9): after prior crizotinib, offer alectinib, brigatinib, lorlatinib, or ceritinib (moderate; strong).[[2]]
The ASCO treatment algorithm covering ALK and other driver alterations is shown here:
[[5]]
Key clinical trial evidence (all used crizotinib as comparator):
[[2]][[6]][[7]][[8]][[9]][[10]][[11]]
The ALEX final overall survival analysis (2025) confirmed sustained long-term systemic and intracranial efficacy, establishing alectinib as a standard of care.[[6]] The following figure from the original ALEX trial shows the progression-free survival, subgroup, CNS progression, and overall survival outcomes:
[[7]]
The CROWN 7-year update reported the longest PFS of any single-agent targeted therapy across metastatic malignancies, with no new intracranial progression events after the first 30 months on lorlatinib—suggesting ALK+ NSCLC may evolve toward a chronic condition in a subset of patients[[8]].[[9]][[11]] The CROWN Kaplan-Meier curves for PFS, intracranial progression, and OS are shown here:
[[12]]
Sequencing and resistance: No head-to-head randomized trials compare alectinib, brigatinib, and lorlatinib in the first line, so selection is individualized by efficacy, CNS burden, comorbidity, and toxicity profile.[[2]][[13]] A Cochrane review confirmed next-generation ALK inhibitors achieve superior PFS and OS versus crizotinib and are standard of care, but could draw no conclusion on optimal sequencing.[[13]] At progression, NCCN and ASCO both emphasize plasma or tissue molecular testing to detect ALK resistance mutations (e.g., G1202R, L1196M) that guide next-line therapy.[[1]]


Emerging evidence presented at the 2026 ASCO Annual Meeting (a network meta-analysis of 15 trials and 4,392 patients) suggests lorlatinib ranks highest for first-line PFS (HR 0.19 vs crizotinib, 95% CrI 0.13–0.27; SUCRA 0.91) and intracranial PFS (HR 0.07), while alectinib showed durable benefit with high-certainty evidence (PFS HR 0.39; OS HR 0.67), supporting current guideline recommendations.[[14]]
